```plato
//==
// # Finite elements
//
// A linear-elastic finite-element analysis, end to end: element stiffness from
// shape-function gradients, assembly into a global system, essential boundary
// conditions and loads, an iterative solve, and the strain / stress readings
// taken back off the answer. Types are in `finite-elements.types.plato`; the
// material record and the beam the 1D path analyses are in
// `engineering.types.plato`.
//
// Two decisions shape everything below, and they are the same decision seen
// twice.
//
// **The assembled matrix is a coordinate-list `SparseMatrix`.** Its stated
// invariant (`matrices.types.plato`) is that the value at a position is the SUM
// of the entries naming it, so concatenating two entry lists is matrix addition.
// Assembly is therefore a `FlatMap` over the elements and nothing else — no
// scatter pass, no accumulation, no ordering requirement, and no mutable global
// matrix. That is the representation a pure language actually wants, and it is
// why nothing here needs a hash map from (row, column) to slot.
//
// **The solve is a conjugate gradient.** It follows from the representation: a
// coordinate list has no random access — `ElementAt` on it is a scan of every
// entry — so any method that indexes the matrix, Gaussian elimination and
// Cholesky included, is quadratic per element read before it does any
// arithmetic. A Krylov method never indexes the matrix; it only ever multiplies
// by it, and that product is one sweep of the entries. Elimination would also
// need pivoting and fill-in, both of which mean rebuilding the storage.
//
// Sections, in order:
//  - System vectors
//  - Sparse system operations
//  - Boundary conditions as vectors
//  - The constrained conjugate gradient
//  - The isotropic element kernel
//  - The linear tetrahedron
//  - The linear triangle
//  - Solid analysis
//  - Plane analysis
//  - Recovering strain and stress
//  - Reading a solution
//  - Euler-Bernoulli beams

library FiniteElements
{
    //==
    // # System vectors
    //
    // A system vector is a plain `Array<Number>`, one entry per degree of
    // freedom. The four operations below are everything the conjugate gradient
    // needs; each is one `Zip` or one fold, so none of them is worth a type.

    // The dot product of two system vectors of the same length.
    SystemDot(a: Array<Number>, b: Array<Number>): Number
        => SumOf(a.Zip(b, (x, y) => x * y));
```
